about: Idea techniques and seeded stimulus pools for the divergence step (H2/H3). A MENU of starting points, never a fence: an option may use any technique listed here, combine two, or use an invented technique named 'invented:<name>' with a one-sentence description. No gate checks membership in this file. scripts/design/seed.py draws from it with a recorded seed; scripts/design/divergence.py validates the result without reading it.

problem_types.design: the look of the whole piece: palette, type, kit, motion character
problem_types.narrative-spine: the order and shape of the story the piece tells
problem_types.explanation: how one hard idea is made understandable to the audience
problem_types.visual-metaphor: the picture that stands for an abstract mechanism
problem_types.structure: how a system, page or figure is divided and connected
problem_types.naming: titles, section names, labels for invented concepts
problem_types.opening: the first seconds or the first screen: the hook
problem_types.strategy: what to include, cut, or risk in the piece
problem_types.technical: how a mechanism actually works, stripped of habit
problem_types.stuck: every option so far feels like the same idea
problem_types.critique: reframing an existing draft that is not working

rules: Divergence runs for PIVOTAL decisions only: the look, the narrative spine, each hero figure, each pivotal scene (opening, payoff). It is not injected into every answer.
Each pivotal decision gets at least three options, each from a DIFFERENT technique. An invented technique with a description counts as a technique.
The generator and the critic are different agents. The critic judges every option against the three rejection tests and writes which test failed and why.
Never lower the bar to reach a count. If no option survives the critic, run a new generation round with techniques not yet used; never re-admit an option the critic rejected.

Randomness is real: techniques and stimuli are drawn by seed.py from random.Random(seed), every draw is recorded, and the same seed replays the same draws. The model does not pick its own 'random' word.

critic_tests.question: Could the user have come up with this alone, in about a minute, without help?
critic_tests.reject_when: the option is the first or second thing a competent person in the user's seat would say

critic_tests.question: Is this a known default, or the usual answer with a new coat of paint?
critic_tests.reject_when: removing the decorative wording leaves the standard template (title card, left-to-right boxes, dark slide with a glowing accent, timeline of releases)

critic_tests.question: Is it surprising but fails to make the subject clearer or the decision better?
critic_tests.reject_when: the novelty cannot be tied to one concrete thing the audience will understand, remember or do because of it

techniques.name: Provocation, then extract the movement
how_to: Name an assumption the subject rests on so firmly that nobody states it.
Write a deliberately unreasonable statement that breaks it, marked as a provocation.
Do not judge the statement. Ask what would have to be true for it to work, and what it would make easy.
Keep the direction the statement pushed you in (the movement), drop the statement itself, and land on something buildable.

example.problem: Opening scene for a video about a job queue that retries failed work.
example.move: Provocation: the queue never fails anything. Movement: failure is a place work visits, not an ending.
example.result: Open on a single job leaving, going round a loop marked 'later', and coming back; the retry policy is introduced as the shape of that loop.

failure_modes: Shipping the provocation literally instead of the movement it pointed to.
A provocation so mild it is just the normal answer phrased as a question.
Stopping at the first movement; the second one is usually the useful one.

techniques.name: Constraint, then relax
how_to: Draw or pick one severe, even absurd, constraint and apply it to the whole piece.
Solve the problem seriously inside the constraint until something works.
Write down what the constraint forced you to discover: the one element that had to survive.
Loosen the constraint to a sensible level while keeping that discovery intact.

example.problem: Look of a page explaining a permissions model with eleven roles.
example.move: Constraint: two colours and no tables. Discovery: roles only differ by what they may NOT touch, so one map of 'forbidden zones' explains all eleven.
example.result: Relaxed: full palette allowed, but the hero figure stays a single map with forbidden zones shaded per role.

failure_modes: Choosing a constraint that changes nothing (a constraint must remove a habit).
Relaxing so far that the discovery is lost and the default returns.
Treating the constraint as the deliverable instead of as a probe.

techniques.name: Inversion
how_to: State the goal of the piece in one sentence.
Ask what would guarantee the goal fails: list the surest ways to confuse, bore or mislead this audience.
Turn each failure into its precise opposite.
Build the option from the most specific opposite, not the most general one.

example.problem: Spine for a walkthrough of a payment reconciliation service.
example.move: Surest failure: explain every component before the viewer knows what can go wrong. Opposite: the viewer sees money go missing first.
example.result: Spine runs from one missing amount, backwards through the components that each could have lost it, ending on the one that did.

failure_modes: Listing generic failures ('too long', 'unclear') whose opposites are platitudes.
Producing a checklist of things to avoid instead of an option to build.

techniques.name: Assumption reversal
how_to: List every assumption the obvious answer depends on, including the boring ones.
Reverse them one at a time: what if this were false?
For each reversal, ask what the piece would look like and what it would reveal.
Keep the reversal that explains the most with the least extra machinery.

example.problem: Hero figure for a caching layer.
example.move: Assumption: the cache sits between the caller and the database. Reversed: the database sits behind the cache's back, as its slow memory.
example.result: Figure drawn from the cache's point of view: a fast desk in front, a far archive behind, and staleness shown as the distance between them.

failure_modes: Reversing an assumption that is false only in rare edge cases nobody needs.
Keeping the reversal as a gimmick without checking it is still accurate to the code.

techniques.name: Analogy by structure, not surface
how_to: Write down the mechanism as relations only: what waits for what, what limits what, what flows where.
Take a distant field (drawn or chosen) and find something in it with the SAME relations.
Check the mapping part by part; every important part must have a counterpart and no counterpart may imply a false behaviour.
Use the analogy only for the parts it maps, and say where it stops.

example.problem: Visual metaphor for back-pressure in a streaming pipeline.
example.move: Relations: a slow consumer must be able to make the producer wait. Field: canal locks. A lock fills only when the next chamber is ready.
example.result: Pipeline drawn as a flight of locks; a stalled lower chamber visibly holds boats in the upper ones. Fence: locks do not drop boats; queues with limits do.

failure_modes: Surface analogy: picked because it looks similar, not because it behaves the same.
No fence: the analogy is stretched to parts where it teaches something false.
A field so familiar to the audience's domain that it is not distant at all.

techniques.name: Role swap with a distant field
how_to: Pick a practitioner from a distant field (drawn or chosen), not a competitor or a near neighbour.
Describe how they actually work: their tools, their checks, what they fear, what they never skip.
Ask how that person would solve this exact problem with their habits.
Bring back the structure of their solution, not the costume.

example.problem: Narrative spine for onboarding engineers to a large monorepo.
example.move: Role: a museum curator. Curators build a route with three anchor objects and let visitors skip everything else.
example.result: Spine is a guided route through three anchor files, each opening a 'room'; every other directory is a labelled door the viewer may leave closed.

failure_modes: Role-play on the surface (a chef 'cooking up' code) with no borrowed method.
Choosing a role whose method is just the standard engineering method renamed.

techniques.name: Time shift
how_to: Solve the problem as it would have been solved long ago, with only the tools of that time.
Solve it as it might be solved far in the future, when today's limits are gone.
Compare the two answers and name what both kept: that is the durable core.
Build the option around the durable core using today's means.

example.problem: Explaining why a service uses idempotency keys.
example.move: Long ago: a clerk stamps each paper order with a number and refuses a second order with the same stamp. Far future: every request carries its own proof of uniqueness.
example.result: Both keep 'the request names itself'. The explanation opens on the clerk's stamp and dissolves into the key header.

failure_modes: Nostalgia or futurism as decoration, with no shared core extracted.
A historical picture that misstates how the real mechanism behaves.

techniques.name: Negative space
how_to: Map what is already present: what the code does, what the docs say, what every explainer of this subject shows.
Look at the gaps: what nobody shows, says, or draws.
Ask why each gap exists; 'nobody thought of it' and 'it is hard to draw' are the valuable answers.
Build the option out of the gap.

example.problem: Hero figure for an authentication flow.
example.move: Every diagram of this flow shows the success path. Nobody draws the time between steps, where tokens expire.
example.result: Hero figure is a timeline of waiting: each step is a short block, and the long gaps between them carry the expiry rules.

failure_modes: Filling a gap that exists because the content does not matter to this audience.
Calling the obvious missing piece 'negative space' when everyone already notices it.

techniques.name: Synthesis that is neither A nor B
how_to: State the two competing options plainly, with what each optimises and what each gives up.
Find the goal they share and the assumption they both make.
Drop the shared assumption and design a third option that reaches the shared goal without either trade-off.
Reject any result that is an average or a split (half of each).

example.problem: Choosing between a dense reference page and a short narrated video.
example.move: Shared goal: the reader can act on the system. Shared assumption: one artefact serves every reader.
example.result: A page whose every section opens with a ten-second clip of the moment it explains; the clip is the hook, the text is the reference.

failure_modes: A compromise (do a bit of both) presented as a synthesis.
Dropping an assumption that is actually a hard requirement.

techniques.name: First principles
how_to: Describe what the subject does at the lowest level that is still true: inputs, outputs, the one rule in between.
Discard every inherited layer (the framework, the usual diagram, the usual vocabulary).
Rebuild the explanation from that rule, adding back only what is logically needed.
Check each re-added piece against the code, not against habit.

example.problem: Explaining a rate limiter to non-engineers.
example.move: Lowest true level: a bucket refills at a fixed speed; each request takes one token; empty means wait.
example.result: The whole explanation is one bucket with a dripping tap, then the code's two numbers labelled on it; nothing about middleware.

failure_modes: Stopping at a level that is still framework vocabulary.
Oversimplifying past the point where the explanation is still true.

techniques.name: Forced combination
how_to: Take the subject and one unrelated form or field (drawn or chosen).
Ask what their offspring would be: a piece that is fully both.
List what the combined form makes possible that neither had alone.
Keep only the combinations that serve the audience's understanding.

example.problem: Look for a video about a deploy pipeline.
example.move: Combine with a railway departure board.
example.result: Each stage is a row that flips like a departure board: on time, delayed, cancelled; the board becomes the recurring motif and the colour roles map to its states.

failure_modes: Combining with something trendy rather than something whose structure helps.
Keeping the combined look while the content stays a standard slide.

techniques.name: Counterfactual (what if it were otherwise)
how_to: State how the system is now.
Pose one large change: the main dependency vanishes, load is a thousand times higher, the user is a machine.
Follow the consequences two or three steps out.
Use the consequence that best reveals why the system is built the way it is.

example.problem: Spine for explaining why a service has a write-ahead log.
example.move: What if the power failed mid-write, every time?
example.result: Spine replays one write three times with the power cut at three points; the log is introduced only when the viewer has seen the corruption it prevents.

failure_modes: A dramatic what-if whose consequences do not touch the real design.
Exploring consequences without returning to the actual system.

techniques.name: Random entry (a drawn word or object)
how_to: Take the drawn word or object exactly as drawn; do not redraw because it seems unhelpful.
Describe its properties and behaviours in detail.
Force at least three connections to the problem; the first is usually surface-level, push past it.
Keep the connection that carries a structural principle, and apply that principle.

example.move: Drawn word: dimmer switch. Properties: continuous, reversible, reachable without rewiring.
example.result: Flags drawn as dimmers on a wall plate, one per feature, with rollout percentage as the dimmer position; a kill switch is a dimmer turned to zero.

failure_modes: Redrawing until a 'convenient' word appears, which defeats the draw.
A cute connection with no principle behind it.

techniques.name: Oblique card
how_to: Draw one oblique instruction from the pool.
Apply it literally to the current draft or problem, however odd it seems.
Note what changed in how you see the problem.
Turn that change into a concrete option.

example.problem: Hero figure for a build cache that keeps coming out as a row of boxes.
example.move: Card drawn: 'Show the waiting, not the doing.'
example.result: The figure becomes a queue of builds waiting on a cold cache, with the cache hit drawn as a thin bypass lane that skips the whole queue.

failure_modes: Interpreting the card so loosely that it changes nothing.
Drawing again because the first card was uncomfortable.

techniques.name: Side door (abandon the obvious path)
how_to: Write down the obvious approach and forbid it.
Enter the problem from an unrelated starting point (a drawn word works).
Ask how that starting point would deal with the problem.
Extract the principle and translate it back into the subject's own terms.

example.problem: Explaining a scheduler that everyone explains with a clock.
example.move: Clock forbidden. Entry: a restaurant ticket rail, where tickets are ordered by when they can be cooked, not when they arrived.
example.result: The scheduler is shown as a ticket rail; priority and readiness become ticket position and colour.

failure_modes: Forbidding the obvious path in words but returning to it in the result.
An entry point so far away that the translation back fails.

techniques.name: Scale shift
how_to: Show the subject at a scale far larger or far smaller than the usual one: one byte, or a whole year of traffic.
Ask what becomes visible at that scale that is invisible at the normal one.
Choose the scale where the key behaviour is most obvious.
Build the figure or scene at that scale, then zoom once to the normal view.

example.problem: Hero figure for a log compaction job.
example.move: Usual scale: one compaction run. Shifted: a month of runs on one strip.
example.result: The figure is a month-long strip where storage grows like a sawtooth; each tooth is one compaction, and the single-run view is an inset.

failure_modes: Choosing a scale for spectacle where the key behaviour is not visible.
Forgetting to return to the scale the audience works at.

techniques.name: Subtraction (remove the element everyone keeps)
how_to: List the elements every version of this piece has (the title card, the architecture box diagram, the summary slide).
Remove the one that seems most essential.
Ask what must now carry its job, and whether that carrier does the job better.
Keep the subtraction if the piece got clearer; otherwise try the next most essential element.

example.problem: Look for a system overview page.
example.move: Removed: the big box-and-arrow architecture diagram at the top.
example.result: The page opens on one request travelling through the system; the architecture is assembled piece by piece as the request reaches each part.

failure_modes: Removing something the audience actually needs to orient themselves.
Subtracting a minor element and calling it bold.

every element enters from the same edge
the whole idea must fit in one frame
no arrows anywhere
only one thing moves in each scene
every shape is a circle
the subject is not named until the last scene
it must work with the sound off
one continuous camera move from start to end
every figure has at most five parts
no diagrams, only physical objects
everything is shown at life size
monochrome plus a single accent used once per scene
the story is told in reverse order
one sentence per scene, at most twelve words
the viewer must make a prediction before each answer
no icons
the page has no headings
start with the failure, not the feature
every label is a verb
titles use only words the user has said
it must be drawable with a pen in thirty seconds
nothing moves except the data
the hero element appears in every frame
the layout is a single grid of nine cells
explain it with exactly three numbers
no metaphors allowed
one type size for everything
the whole piece is one zoom from far to near
show it only as a timeline
every scene ends on a question
the empty state is the hero
use only things found on a kitchen table
the narrator speaks as the system itself
no element may be bigger than a quarter of the frame
it has to be understood by someone standing three metres away
the explanation fits on the back of a ticket

Replace the obvious picture with its shadow.

Slow the important moment down ten times.
Show the waiting, not the doing.
Let the viewer find it before you say it.
Swap the foreground and the background.
Draw it from inside the machine.
Say it twice; the second time with half the words.
What does the thing refuse to do?
Use one honest number instead of five.
Find the moment of surprise and build backwards from it.
